## How we work here

**awpredict** — Predict what your environment does next, and how surprised you were — is one of several open repositories cut from the same
system. They share one set of engineering rules, and those rules are published:

> **This repository is a mirror.** It is published from the AitherOS monorepo
> by a sync lane that overwrites the files here on every sync, so a change only
> sticks once it lands at the source. Issues and pull requests here are the way
> to propose one.

### 📖 [The Developer Codex](https://aitherium.github.io/awskills/codex.html) — read this first

Eighteen laws for building software that tells you when it is wrong, plus a
four-chapter ramp if you have never worked with a coding agent before. Every law
was a real failure first, and every number in it was counted rather than
estimated. [Read the source](https://github.com/Aitherium/awskills/tree/main/codex).

The parts, in the order they will bite you:

| part | what it covers |
|---|---|
| **Enforcement** | a standard nothing checks is a preference |
| **Silence** | the expensive failures return 200 and log nothing |
| **Adoption** | a gate that floods gets switched off |
| **Deployment** | written is not deployed |
| **Trust** | fail closed, then prove the happy path |

### The one rule that decides whether a pull request lands

> **A change is done when a check that could have failed passes.**

Not "the tests are green" and not "it looks right". Name the command that goes
red when your change is wrong, and show its output. If no such command exists,
writing it *is* the contribution — very often the most valuable one.

### The loop we actually run

```
something breaks
  → you fix it
  → you ask: could a check have caught this?
  → if yes, THE CHECK IS THE WORK. Write it, watch it fail on purpose,
    wire it somewhere unattended. Do not open a ticket.
```

### Before you open a pull request

1. **Run the checks this repo ships.** They are the contract, not a formality.
2. **Watch your new check fail.** A gate nobody has seen fail is not a gate — break
   the thing on purpose, confirm it goes red, put it back.
3. **State one weakness of your own change.** An untested assumption, a case you
   did not cover, a number you did not verify. Reviewers find it anyway; saying it
   first is faster and it is how everyone here is expected to work.

This is a small, research-stage package. Contributions are welcome —
especially another negative result, a bug in the engines, or a new
`EnvironmentAdapter` for a domain we haven't tried.

## Setup

```bash
pip install -e ".[torch]"
python -m pytest tests/ -v
```

## Ground rules

- **Degrade loudly, never silently.** An engine that can't operate (torch
  missing, checkpoint unreadable) sets `ok = False` and returns `None`/`[]`
  from its methods — it must never raise into a caller's turn loop, and it
  must never fabricate a prediction. This is the one rule every PR is held
  to; see `RESULTS.md` for why it mattered more than any architecture choice.
- **A trainer needs a positive assertion, not just a passing shape test.** A
  test that only checks a training method returns the right dict keys cannot
  tell a fitted model from a randomly-initialized one. If you add or change
  training code, assert it actually reduces loss on a target it can fit —
  see `tests/test_value_head.py` for the pattern.
- **New engine or adapter code should carry its own test file**, not rely on
  the existing ones happening to exercise it.

## Reporting a result

If you run this against your own environment and get a result — positive or
negative — open an issue or a PR adding it to `RESULTS.md`. Negative results
that survive someone trying to break them are the most useful thing this
repo can publish.
